# Alternatives to Electron

There are credible alternatives, but the right shortlist depends on what you want to retain: an HTML/CSS/JavaScript interface, Node.js integration, or only the product's behavior. No concrete platform, performance, deployment, or licensing requirement was provided, so the ranking below is an order for investigation, not a claim that one framework is universally superior. I have not benchmarked or deployed these candidates.

## Ranked shortlist

1. **Tauri** — A close architectural alternative when retaining a web interface matters. Its Rust core manages native operations and communicates with system WebViews. The official documentation names different engines on Windows, macOS, and Linux, making platform testing a central tradeoff. It is not an Electron API replacement.
   Source: https://tauri.app/concept/process-model/

2. **Wails** — Particularly relevant when Go is an acceptable backend language. Its public v2 example embeds frontend assets and exposes Go methods to JavaScript through generated bindings. This gives a concrete route to reuse web UI code while replacing application-side integration. Budget for rewriting Electron/Node integration and checking WebView compatibility. The live FAQ now describes v3; do not mix version-specific guidance.
   Sources: https://github.com/wailsapp/wails/blob/master/website/docs/howdoesitwork.mdx and https://wails.io/faq/

3. **Neutralinojs** — Another option for keeping JavaScript, HTML, and CSS while using the operating system's browser library. Its architecture includes a local static server and a WebSocket bridge for native operations; extensions can communicate with other languages. Check the native operations you need before committing, since an Electron API surface cannot be assumed.
   Source: https://neutralino.js.org/docs/

4. **Avalonia** — A stronger change of UI stack: .NET with C# or F# and XAML, using Avalonia's own renderer. It is relevant if the aim is to build a desktop interface without depending on a web UI. Existing HTML components would need replacement, and exact operating-system support tiers deserve attention.
   Sources: https://docs.avaloniaui.net/docs/welcome and https://docs.avaloniaui.net/docs/supported-platforms

5. **Flutter desktop** — Relevant when a UI rewrite is acceptable, especially if Flutter is already part of the team's stack. Official documentation supports Windows, macOS, and Linux builds and desktop plugins. Check that required integrations have desktop implementations; the existence of a package for another Flutter platform is insufficient.
   Source: https://docs.flutter.dev/platform-integration/desktop

6. **Qt Quick** — A QML UI toolkit with C++ integration, useful when you can replace a browser interface with a different application UI architecture. Its official module documentation covers visual components, input, models, animation, and extension through C++. This entails a substantive UI migration; assess packaging and applicable licensing for the actual modules you select.
   Source: https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/qtquick-index.html

7. **NW.js** — Worth considering if preserving web technologies and Node.js modules is more important than changing the runtime model. Its official site documents direct Node.js access from DOM code and support for Windows, macOS, and Linux. Choosing it alone does not establish a footprint or memory advantage over Electron.
   Source: https://nwjs.io/

## Do teams commonly return from Tauri to Electron?

This search does not establish that they commonly do. Migration-related search hits show that the question arises, but they provide no representative denominator, migration rate, or controlled comparison. Some discussion snippets appeared potentially related to the excluded source question and were excluded. A migration feasibility document appeared in an independent public-code result, but its attempted raw-page retrieval was blocked; I do not treat it as proof of a completed migration.

There is a credible technical reason a particular team might prefer Electron after evaluating a system-WebView approach: it may require rendering behavior or integrations that are costly to support across different WebViews. Tauri's own documentation explicitly makes platform differences part of the tradeoff. That explains a possible engineering decision; it does not establish how often teams make it.

For an actual choice, build one representative workflow in the strongest alternative for the team's language skills. Exercise the target operating systems, the least portable native integration, and the real packaging/update path. Compare measured installer size, startup, memory under the same workload, UI behavior, accessibility needs, and maintenance effort. These are proposed evaluation criteria, not measured findings from this run. With no concrete problem in the existing Electron approach, there is insufficient information to justify a migration.

## Evidence limits

The discovery used eight literal queries, including one unsuccessful unauthenticated grep.app code-search attempt, and seventeen document-open attempts including failures and repeated section reads. Public code was subsequently accessed through web-indexed GitHub results; that is code-through-web fallback, not native code-search success. Seven candidates were retained without padding the list.

The cutoff is 2026-08-28. The Tauri document reports an update on 2025-02-22 and the Avalonia welcome document reports 2026-04-20. Other candidate evidence is undated live documentation or moving-branch code and is marked date unknown; a current page is not evidence that its current version existed at the cutoff. No cross-framework benchmark, deployment success, or population-level migration claim has been established.

For a solution constrained to 11 August 2016, I would investigate QOwnNotes with a synced Markdown folder and an Android Markdown editor first. It has the strongest opened evidence for keeping your notes as independent files while providing a desktop tagging interface. Tag portability is the part that needs deliberate setup. If later products are admissible, Obsidian is a close match to the requested editing model, but its release dates make it unsuitable as a historical 2016 answer.

1. **QOwnNotes plus file synchronization and an Android Markdown editor.** The [official README](https://github.com/pbek/QOwnNotes/blob/main/README.md) describes an open-source macOS application whose notes remain ordinary Markdown files and can be synchronized through a file-sync service. A [May 2016 integration discussion](https://github.com/pbek/QOwnNotes/issues/177) explains using Android editors and shows a script that puts tag names into filenames so they remain searchable outside QOwnNotes. That is useful but different from your preferred hashtags in the body. A [current tagging-hook example](https://github.com/pbek/QOwnNotes/blob/main/docs/scripting/examples/note-tagging.qml) manages @tags inside note text; adapting it to #tags is a possible implementation task, not a verified out-of-the-box solution. I have not established when that hook became available, and I would not backdate the current native Android app.

2. **Simplenote.** Its [March 2016 announcement](https://simplenote.com/2016/03/29/simplenote-for-windows-and-linux/) confirms Mac and Android clients, tags, and Markdown support in the new Windows/Linux apps. [Current help](https://simplenote.com/help/) describes Markdown on Android and Electron and data export including notes and tags; Android exports JSON, while desktop export creates a ZIP. This is a candidate if portable export is enough for you. It is less direct than editing your own shared directory, and the opened historical source does not establish native Mac Markdown support or body hashtags.

3. **Obsidian — later evidence.** The [official site](https://obsidian.md/) describes local plain-text Markdown files. Its [roadmap](https://obsidian.md/roadmap/) documents hashtag-style nested tags, Android/iOS applications and Live Preview, the latter rendering content while editing. These features closely address your file ownership, tagging and editor requirements. The same roadmap dates its initial release to March 2020, mobile apps to July 2021 and Live Preview to November 2021. It therefore belongs in a later comparison, not a recommendation available on the question date. I have not verified a particular Mac build or Dropbox-on-Android setup.

4. **Joplin — current, undated evidence.** The [official overview](https://joplinapp.org/help/) documents an open-source application with Markdown notes, tags, macOS and Android clients, Evernote import, offline availability and sync options including Dropbox and Nextcloud. It is a useful all-in-one candidate. The overview alone does not prove that the working store is an ordinary Markdown folder, that tags are in the note bodies, or that its features existed by August 2016. Those are material remaining checks before choosing it for your precise requirements.

5. **nvALT plus a separately chosen Android file editor — current behavior is later evidence.** The [current project documentation](https://brettterpstra.com/projects/nvalt/) supports a Mac-side workflow using plain Markdown files, preview and tags. It documents body-hashtag search, but stores assigned tags as Finder metadata, so Android tag interoperability is not automatic. The page is explicitly updated in November 2026 and says the current 3.0 line removed Simplenote sync. A [2011 progress post](https://brettterpstra.com/2011/01/18/nvalt-1-0-8-progress/) confirms earlier Markdown-preview work but treats Simplenote tag sync as unfinished. I would not transfer the current feature set back to 2016.

6. **TagSpaces — partial alternative mechanism.** Its [October 2015 release post](https://www.tagspaces.org/blog/tagspaces-2-0-released/) documents file tagging, Markdown viewers and an Android version. This suggests organizing your notes as files with a tagging file manager, while leaving editing to a suitable editor. The [February 2016 release](https://www.tagspaces.org/blog/tagspaces-2-1-released/) confirms continued availability before the cutoff. Exact Markdown editing, macOS packaging and portable tag representation were not established in the opened material, so this remains a component to evaluate rather than a complete replacement recommendation.

For the file-based routes, I would make a small test collection with representative tags and formatting, open the same files on both devices, and verify that the text and tag convention remain usable independently of either application. I did not run or install these applications. The unauthenticated code-search endpoint was inaccessible; actual public QOwnNotes source was subsequently inspected through web-indexed code.

I would shortlist **SoapUI Open Source** first and **Milkman** second, but I cannot honestly certify either as meeting every requirement from the documentation I found. The main unresolved details are direct OpenAPI import from an arbitrary URL and, for Milkman, the precise workspace file round trip.

### 1. SoapUI Open Source

Its grouping and automation model fits your workflow well. Treat each API or test grouping as a SoapUI project. You can keep multiple projects and switch between separate workspaces. Projects save their contents in XML and can be imported again, so they can be kept in version control. If a project references external files, retain those files alongside it; a workspace file alone is not the complete portable bundle. See the [project documentation](https://www.soapui.org/docs/getting-started/projects/working-with-projects/) and [workspace documentation](https://www.soapui.org/docs/getting-started/working-with-soapui/managing-workspaces/).

The command-line runner can execute every test in a project, or narrow execution to a suite or case using its selection arguments. The practical mapping is to put the imported requests into test cases; a case containing the desired request gives you selective execution. This is a native CLI route, so Postman export is unnecessary for that configuration. I am not claiming that one runner invocation executes every project in a SoapUI workspace. The [runner reference](https://www.soapui.org/docs/automation/cli/functional-tests/) and [Open Source automation features](https://www.soapui.org/docs/open-source/features/) document the relevant behavior.

The important limitation is specification support. The [Swagger/OpenAPI page](https://www.soapui.org/docs/rest-testing/openapi-swagger-support/) lists OpenAPI/Swagger 2.0 for Open Source 5.7.0, with bundled-plugin support for 1.x/2.0 in earlier versions. The [REST service guide](https://www.soapui.org/docs/rest-testing/working-with-rest-services/) shows generated request structure and distinguishes ReadyAPI's OpenAPI 3.0 support. Therefore, do not choose the free Open Source edition on the assumption that it supports a 3.x specification.

I also could not confirm arbitrary Swagger/OpenAPI URL import from these pages: they explicitly describe file and SwaggerHub import. Another page's URL example concerns WADL, which does not prove the OAS requirement. This is a verification gap, not evidence that URL import is impossible.

**Verdict:** a promising complete alternative if your specification version and direct URL import are supported. Those details need checking before treating it as a full match. Its basic documented test execution does not require the optional paid report features.

### 2. Milkman with its HTTP and CLI plugins

[Milkman](https://milkman.dev/docs/) is a JavaFX request workbench with workspaces, collections and requests. Its [public repository](https://github.com/warmuuh/milkman) identifies an MIT license. That makes it especially relevant to your dissatisfaction with Electron-based clients, although a different toolkit alone does not establish good platform-specific UX.

The [HTTP plugin documentation](https://milkman.dev/docs/plugins/rest/) lists an OpenAPI 3.0 importer. The [CLI documentation](https://milkman.dev/docs/plugins/cli/) describes interactive and non-interactive execution of named requests, including workspace/collection/request paths. That supports the selected-request branch of your CLI requirement. I did not find confirmation of a single whole-workspace command.

Two essential details remain unresolved: whether the importer accepts your arbitrary OAS URL and creates the complete request set, and whether a workspace can be exported to disk and reimported intact. Git synchronization is documented, but it is not by itself proof of the file import/export operation you requested. Likewise, the HTTP plugin's planned format exporters should not be confused with evidence that the core application cannot persist workspaces. Postman import does not establish Postman export.

**Verdict:** keep it on the evaluation list, especially if the UI approach matters, but verify the URL-to-workspace-to-file round trip before adopting it. I have not confirmed every required capability in a free complete workflow.

### Scope of this recommendation

These are documentation-based findings, not installation or execution results. Your question is dated 8 January 2020. Milkman's opened web documentation explicitly shows 2022 and 2024 modification dates, while the SoapUI pages and repository overview are undated live material. They do not establish which exact capabilities were available at the original question date.

I have kept unknowns visible rather than interpreting missing documentation as a decisive failure. If the actual specification is OpenAPI 3.x, SoapUI Open Source's documented format scope becomes a concrete mismatch; if it is Swagger/OpenAPI 2.0 and direct URL import works, SoapUI is the stronger documented starting point.

candidate_links.name: Milkman with HTTP and CLI plugins

Yes. For the plain English/ASCII input you describe, GNU tr is the most direct ready-to-use solution. If you want a newly randomized result on each run, a short Python standard-library filter gives you more control.

## 1. GNU tr: preserve the text's structure exactly

GNU tr performs character-by-character translation and is GPL-licensed. Its dated coreutils 8.32 manual documents the required operation: [tr manual](https://manpages.debian.org/bullseye/coreutils/tr.1.en.html).

For example, apply ROT13 only to letters:

```sh
LC_ALL=C tr 'A-Za-z' 'N-ZA-Mn-za-m' < input.txt > gibberish.txt
```

For ASCII input, this preserves every word's length, the uppercase/lowercase pattern, punctuation, spaces, tabs, and line breaks. “Hello, world!” becomes “Uryyb, jbeyq!”. These preservation properties follow from replacing each ASCII letter with exactly one letter of the same case and leaving every other character outside the translation sets.

The output is deterministic, and applying the command twice restores the original. That is useful for producing visually similar nonsense, but it is not a random-word generator and should not be treated as secure concealment. Exact pixel widths in a proportional font can still change, even when character counts do not.

## 2. Python's standard library: randomize each letter

The [random.choice documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/random.html#random.choice) supplies the only random-selection primitive needed. This small filter uses bytes so that punctuation and line-ending bytes pass through unchanged:

```python
import random
import sys

lower = b"abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz"
upper = b"ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"

def replace(c):
    if 97 <= c <= 122:
        return random.choice(lower)
    if 65 <= c <= 90:
        return random.choice(upper)
    return c

sys.stdout.buffer.write(
    bytes(replace(c) for c in sys.stdin.buffer.read())
)
```

Save it as gibberish.py and run:

```sh
python3 gibberish.py < input.txt > gibberish.txt
```

This preserves the same structural properties as the tr command while selecting new replacement letters on each run. It needs no third-party library. It can occasionally produce an ordinary word, and the result will not necessarily be pronounceable. This is a proposed wrapper derived from the documented primitive; I did not execute it during this search.

## 3. Gibberify: an alternative component for pronounceable output

[Gibberify](https://github.com/brisvag/gibberify) is a GPL-3.0 Python project with graphical, command-line and importable-library interfaces. It builds gibberish using syllables, so it is worth considering when language-like output matters.

However, I could not verify that it preserves word lengths, punctuation and line breaks. The README does not make that guarantee, and its approach can change word lengths. It would need a wrapper or adaptation to meet your layout requirement reliably. I would choose tr or the small Python filter first for the exact request.

## Evidence limits

The GNU manual's underlying source is dated September 2020, before the question's 2022-09-22 cutoff. Python 3.10.7 has an [official release date of 2022-09-06](https://www.python.org/downloads/release/python-3107/), but attempts to retrieve its historical API documentation failed; the opened API documentation is live, so I have not treated that page as historical evidence. Gibberify's precise pre-cutoff status also remains unverified.

An unauthenticated grep.app code-search request was inaccessible. I used public GitHub code indexed through web search as a fallback, not as evidence of successful native code search.

candidate_links.name: GNU coreutils tr with an ASCII letter substitution
Python standard library random.choice with a byte-preserving filter

# A Q&A framework shortlist

**Question2Answer is the strongest first prototype for the stated PHP/MySQL preference.** It already addresses much of the core Q&A model, while Askbot is the most useful complete alternative found if Python is acceptable. I would evaluate the remaining requirements as concrete integrations before choosing a platform.

The decision date is **28 February 2014**. The sources below mix dated historical releases and current documentation. I distinguish them because a present-day feature list cannot establish what was available in 2014. These are candidates for evaluation; none has been deployed or tested in this research.

## Ranked candidates

### 1. Question2Answer — primary framework

[Official documentation](https://docs.question2answer.org/) describes PHP/MySQL, categories and tags, voting, reputation points, translation, differentiated user roles and plugin customization. That is a strong match to the preferred stack and core community workflow.

The [dated version history](https://docs.question2answer.org/install/versions/1/) establishes version 1.6.3 on 19 January 2014. Its 2013 entries document question view counters, per-category privileges, moderation based on points, uploaded-content storage and an image-upload API. They also document security fixes and CSRF protection. This supports treating Q2A as a real pre-decision candidate, while avoiding the assumption that every modern feature existed then.

I would still verify arbitrary file attachments, mathematics authoring, badge compatibility and reporting. Image upload is narrower than accepting arbitrary attachments; a view counter is narrower than a weekly operational dashboard. The project's scaling and security descriptions are useful leads, but do not establish capacity or security under a particular workload.

### 2. Askbot — complete Python/Django alternative

[Askbot](https://www.askbot.com/) is worth comparing when Python is an acceptable development stack. Its current official site describes tags, voting, accepted answers, reputation-based privileges, badges, moderation and a multilingual interface.

There is useful historical evidence: [Askbot 0.7.49 on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/askbot/0.7.49/) was released on 19 September 2013. Its version-specific description confirms votes, reputation, user levels and combined text/tag search, and identifies the software as GPLv3. That package recommends PostgreSQL and specifies old Django/Python requirements and a MyISAM constraint for MySQL.

This makes Askbot a concrete historical alternative, but it does not prove that the old version covered every requested feature. Mathematics, attachments, badges and reporting deserve version-specific checks. Integrating it into an existing Django application also had documented limitations.

### 3. Question2Answer Badges plugin — fill the gamification gap

The [Q2A Badges plugin](https://github.com/NoahY/q2a-badges) provides configurable achievement badges, award notifications and badge displays on profiles and posts. Its README also describes translation and hooks for custom badges. This is a direct extension of the first candidate, rather than a separate forum.

The README labels it beta. Compatibility with the selected Q2A release and the required award rules needs verification. I did not establish a dated release before February 2014, so its historical availability remains unknown.

### 4. Drupal Answers — modular CMS alternative

[Drupal Answers](https://www.drupal.org/project/answers) assembles questions and answers with supporting accepted-answer, voting, reputation and tagging modules. It is worth considering when the project also needs a broader CMS and the developer is willing to assemble the workflow.

The present project page warns about incompatible version changes and reports no supported stable releases. I could not verify a dated historical feature snapshot, so this is an architecture alternative with substantial integration and version-selection caveats.

### 5. AnswerHub — commercial comparison point

[AnswerHub's official developer documentation](https://developer.answerhub.com/) describes role-based permissions, moderation, built-in badges and reputation, plus REST APIs, plugins and themes. Those capabilities make it relevant to a purchase-versus-development comparison.

I did not verify pricing or a complete match for mathematical editing, multilingual operation, attachments and reporting. A targeted demonstration and written feature scope would be needed to judge whether paying reduces enough implementation work. The live documentation does not establish the exact feature set offered in February 2014.

### 6. Q2A WYSIWYG Math Editor — later mathematical-authoring component

The [Q2A WYSIWYG Math Editor repository](https://github.com/fardina/q2a-wysiwyg-matheditor) shows a CKEditor-based approach to editing mathematical formulas and rendering them with MathJax. It is a relevant implementation path for the LaTeX-oriented authoring requirement.

The inspected README explicitly discusses a September 2019 update and testing with Q2A 1.8.2. This is **post-decision evidence**, not proof of an available solution in February 2014. Version compatibility and the exact editor/rendering integration still need checking.

## How I would evaluate the choice

For Q2A, I would build a small representative workflow: create a tagged question, post and accept an answer, vote, earn reputation, exercise moderator permissions, upload the required file types and author a realistic formula. Then I would produce the requested weekly answer count and page-visit report. These are proposed acceptance checks, not completed tests.

The [official Q2A plugin catalogue](https://docs.question2answer.org/addons/plugins/) confirms that extension routes exist for badges and mathematics, but its live entries do not date those routes to 2014. Translation of interface text also needs to be distinguished from a community containing multiple content languages. Ease of development and scalability depend on the chosen version, plugins, hosting and actual workload; the reviewed sources do not settle those questions.

A public unauthenticated grep.app code-search attempt was inaccessible. I therefore used **code-through-web** discovery of public GitHub repositories, not a successful native code-search session. I also inspected OSQA's public repository, but did not obtain enough dated feature evidence to rank it above the six candidates here.

For more than 10,000 tasks lasting 30 seconds to one hour, I would use a durable job registry and a bounded pool of workers. The crucial requirements are a stable identity for each logical task, exclusive ownership while it runs, and a completion record that survives worker failure.

There is a failure case to resolve explicitly: a worker can perform an effect and crash before acknowledging completion. A queue may then retry the task. Consequently, a queue's deduplication feature is not by itself a guarantee that arbitrary task code physically executes only once. Celery's acknowledgment documentation and AWS's FIFO explanation both describe this boundary. The practical goal is one accepted logical job and one committed logical result, using idempotent effects or an appropriate transaction.

Ranked candidates

1. PostgreSQL job ledger with a unique job key, ON CONFLICT, and FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.5/sql-select.html
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.5/sql-insert.html

This is my strongest starting point if the application already uses PostgreSQL. A unique key prevents two producer attempts from registering the same logical task; workers claim different pending rows transactionally. For hour-long tasks, my proposed design uses a short claim transaction followed by a renewable lease, rather than holding a database transaction open throughout the computation. Completion must verify current ownership. Database results can be committed with the completion record; external operations need their own idempotency contract. The opened 9.5 release notes establish the underlying SQL features on 2016-01-07, although today's versioned documentation is not an archived 2016 page.
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.5/release-9-5.html

2. Amazon SQS FIFO queues.
https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/developer/how-the-amazon-sqs-fifo-api-works/

Use a stable MessageDeduplicationId for submission retries, enough MessageGroupIds to permit independent jobs to run concurrently, and extend visibility while a worker is active. The 2016 article documents a five-minute producer deduplication window and acknowledges that processing can repeat after visibility expires. An hour-long runtime therefore needs visibility management; permanent submission or completion deduplication still belongs in a durable application ledger. This is a plausible managed dispatch layer, with supporting evidence dated 2016-11-21.

3. Celery 4.2 with RabbitMQ.
https://docs.celeryq.dev/en/v4.2.0/userguide/tasks.html

Celery supplies task execution, broker integration and separate worker routing for long and short tasks. Pair it with the unique job registry described above. Choose acknowledgments deliberately: acknowledging before execution risks unfinished work after a crash, while late acknowledgment requires safely repeatable tasks. The documented worker-loss exceptions also matter when configuring recovery. Celery is a task runner, not sufficient proof of unique registration. Version 4.2.0 is confirmed before the cutoff by its 2018-06-10 package release.
https://pypi.org/project/celery/4.2.0/

4. Celery Once / QueueOnce.
https://github.com/cameronmaske/celery-once

This is a focused addition to Celery for rejecting another pending or running invocation with the same task identity. The public implementation acquires a lock before submission and normally releases it after the task returns. Configure the identity to match the business task and make the timeout cover both queue waiting and execution; the documented one-hour default is a poor automatic fit for a task that may itself run for an hour. It does not replace permanent result deduplication. The inspected implementation is current and undated, so historical availability remains unverified.
https://github.com/cameronmaske/celery-once/blob/master/celery_once/tasks.py

5. Bull.
https://github.com/OptimalBits/bull/blob/develop/REFERENCE.md

For Node.js with Redis, Bull's regular jobId check suppresses another retained job with the same ID, and renewable locks coordinate active workers. Retain completed identities for the required deduplication horizon, or keep a separate ledger. Its stalled-job recovery can run work again, and CPU-heavy handlers can disrupt lease renewal. Those are material constraints for long computations. The current reference verifies these mechanisms, but I have not established a dated version available by the question's cutoff.

6. pg-boss.
https://github.com/timgit/pg-boss

For Node.js already using PostgreSQL, pg-boss packages the database-claim approach behind job submission and worker APIs. The opened project introduction specifically confirms SKIP LOCKED claims and concurrent workers. It is a useful implementation to inspect before writing a custom database queue. The page examined does not establish every deduplication or long-job setting, and I would retain explicit business-key and result constraints. Its exact historical feature set was not verified.

Configuration I would carry forward

Assign a deterministic business job ID before enqueueing. Record that ID durably with a uniqueness constraint, and retain its completion identity for as long as repeated registration must be rejected. Run a bounded number of workers sized to actual CPU, memory and I/O requirements; the count of queued jobs alone does not determine capacity.

For each claimed task, record an owner and a deadline, renew ownership while running, and reject completion from an expired owner. Retry abandoned work only under an explicit policy. Treat the side effect and completion record as one transaction when they share a database; otherwise use an idempotency key understood by the external destination. This ownership-and-result design is my synthesis, not a claim that every listed tool implements it automatically.

Before selecting a stack, verify behavior when a worker dies after producing its result but before acknowledgment, when a lease expires while an old worker is still alive, and when a producer repeats a submission after the deduplication window. No capacity benchmark or deployment was performed here.

Search limitations: the unauthenticated grep.app code-search attempt was blocked. Public code was subsequently found through web-indexed GitHub results and inspected through GitHub HTML; this was code-through-web, not successful native code search. Six candidates were retained rather than padding the list, with 8 of 12 queries and 14 of 20 open attempts used. Current, undated evidence has not been silently backdated.

I would start with **Publii** for a straightforward personal blog, or **Ghost** if you want a publishing application running on your server. The most useful distinction is how you want to write and publish: a desktop editor that uploads a static site, a server CMS, or a build workflow.

### 1. Publii — my first option for a simple personal blog

Publii is an open-source desktop CMS. You write locally using a visual or Markdown editor, and publish the generated site to your own hosting. Its static output avoids needing a CMS application or database on the public web server. [Official overview](https://getpublii.com/)

Its documented SEO controls include titles and descriptions, canonical/indexing settings, sitemaps, and structured data. FTP/SFTP and manual file deployment are supported. This makes it a particularly relevant option if you want an editing interface without maintaining a server-side publishing stack. [Features and publishing options](https://getpublii.com/features/)

The important fit question is whether desktop authoring suits you. The blog is self-hosted, but the authoring application runs on your computer. Your summary does not require a browser-based admin interface, so I would keep Publii on the shortlist.

### 2. Ghost — for a server-based publishing system with integrated SEO

Ghost documents automatic metadata, XML sitemaps, canonical tags and structured data. That is a strong match for wanting basic technical SEO handled within the publishing system. [Ghost SEO documentation](https://ghost.org/help/seo/)

Ghost is open source and supports installation on your own VPS. Its self-hosting guide also makes the operational tradeoff clear: installation, software updates and server upkeep are yours to manage. The documented stack includes Node.js and MySQL. Choose it if that administration is acceptable; the writing experience and the hosting effort are separate parts of simplicity. [Self-hosting documentation](https://docs.ghost.org/hosting/)

### 3. WordPress.org — a conventional, extensible alternative

The self-hosted WordPress software supports personal blogs, ordinary post/page editing, GPL licensing and baseline SEO. Its official feature guide describes plugins for finer SEO control. It is worth considering if you want flexibility beyond a narrowly focused blog, while keeping your initial theme and extension choices small. [Features](https://wordpress.org/about/features/)

You will be running a PHP/database application; consult the requirements for the release and host you actually choose. I have not validated a particular theme or SEO-plugin combination. [Hosting requirements](https://wordpress.org/about/requirements/)

### 4. Hugo — for a static blog if you are comfortable with a build workflow

Hugo explicitly supports personal blogs and deployment to your own host. Its official repository identifies the Apache-2.0 license, and its documentation and public template source confirm built-in sitemap generation. [Introduction](https://gohugo.io/about/introduction/) · [Source repository](https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo) · [Sitemap documentation](https://gohugo.io/templates/sitemap/) · [Sitemap source](https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/blob/master/tpl/tplimpl/embedded/templates/sitemap.xml)

I would keep it as a conditional choice: inspect the selected theme's generated titles, descriptions and canonical URLs before calling that exact setup SEO-ready. The research established sitemap support, not the complete SEO behavior of every Hugo theme. A positive check would resolve that uncertainty; otherwise the templates need adjustment or replacement.

**My choice from the information given:** try Publii first if desktop editing works for you. Prefer Ghost when you want the publishing application on your server and can handle its upkeep. WordPress is a broader alternative; Hugo makes more sense when a build-and-deploy workflow already feels simple to you.

These are documentation-based recommendations, not installation tests or guarantees of search rankings. The supplied question is dated 21 September 2024, while this research used current public pages: Publii's homepage and the Hugo documentation show 2026 updates, and other relied-on pages are undated. I have not established exact historical feature parity. No operating-system, budget, browser-editor, or specific-license restriction was added to your summary.
